about: CHAIN great_army_865 (Design/content/CHAINS.md; page Design/content/chains/great_army_865.md; words Data/writing/chain_great_army_865.json). The great heathen army in England from 865: a Frisian shipman who trades at the army's scales, ransoms its captives and a golden gospel book, can warn King Alfred before Twelfth Night 878, and ends as one of the merchants allowed to cross between the two armies. Fourteen cards, 865 to 880 (endings may be taken to 890). Part of the spine's thread price_of_england: its flags en_paid_share and en_hostage_given are set here. Step flags ch_great_army_865_1 .. _10; road flags _camp, _english, _scales, _boy, _plate, _book_word, _book_bought, _gold, _book_home, _book_lost, _skimmed, _reeve, _tofi, _warn, _warned, _unheard; lasting costs _cost_church and _cost_danes. Endings: ch_great_army_865_end_ransomer and ch_great_army_865_end_line (what happened), ch_great_army_865_end_warned (history changed: changed_chippenham_warned), ch_great_army_865_end_camp (with changed_codex_aureus_lost if the book was lost); each sets ch_great_army_865_done, so a house has one ending. Steps 1 to 5 and 8 can each begin the chain. Every option's note names its outcome text. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

cards.note: Step 1, one of the five ways in (drawn in a Kentish port from August 865 to April 866). The heathen army on Thanet and Kent's promise of money. Source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 865 (the army sat on Thanet and made peace with the men of Kent, who promised money; under cover of the peace and the promise the army stole away by night and ravaged all eastern Kent). Whether this force was the same as the great army that wintered in East Anglia is not certain (?). Folding balances and silver by weight: the Torksey camp finds. Toki and the reeve are invented. Sets ch_great_army_865_1; the spine's en_paid_share on 'pay'; ch_great_army_865_camp on 'sell'; ch_great_army_865_english on 'pay'.

cards.note: Step 2, and a way in (scheduled by step 1; drawn at Gipeswic or Dommoc from October 865 to October 866). The winter camp among the East Angles. Source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 866 (a great heathen army took winter quarters among the East Angles and were horsed there, and the East Angles made peace with them). The camp as a market with lead weights, hack-silver and dirhams: the finds at Torksey (winter camp of 872-873) and Aldwark, read back to 866 (?). The ertog and the ore: lore/law_tolls.md. The size of the fleet is not recorded. Toki and King Edmund's man are invented. Sets ch_great_army_865_2 (and _1); _scales, _camp or _english by the choice.

cards.note: Step 4, and a way in (scheduled by step 3; drawn at Gipeswic or Dommoc from November 869 to the end of 870). King Edmund killed. Source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 870 for the winter of 869-870 (the army rode over Mercia into East Anglia and took winter quarters at Thetford; that winter King Edmund fought against them, and the Danes had the victory and slew the king and overran all the land); the day, 20 November 869, is the feast kept later (nine days after Martinmas). How he died is told first by Abbo of Fleury about 985, a century on: the priest here will not tell it. Church plate 240 d the piece in goods_793.json. The priest and the sale of plate are invented. cards.note: Step 5, and a way in (scheduled by step 4; drawn at Lundenwic from October 871 to the end of 872). The army's winter in London and the golden gospel book. Sources: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 872 (the army went from Reading to London and took winter quarters there, and the Mercians made peace with them); Bishop Waerferth of Worcester's lease of land at Nuthurst for twenty mancuses of gold, because of the heavy tribute of the barbarians in the year the heathens stayed in London (charter S 1278, of 872; from memory (?)); pennies in Halfdan's name with the London monogram, dating disputed (?). The book is the Codex Aureus now at Stockholm: its Old English inscription says the ealdorman Alfred and Werburg his wife got it from the heathen army with pure gold and gave it to Christ Church. Where and when the army held it is not recorded: the game puts it in the London camp (?). Sets ch_great_army_865_5 (and _1); _book_word, _book_bought (and _camp), or the spine's en_paid_share.

cards.note: Step 6 (scheduled by step 5; drawn at Fordwic, Canterbury's landing, 871 to 874). The ealdorman Alfred and Werburg. Source: the inscription on folio 11 of the Stockholm Codex Aureus (Alfred the ealdorman and Werburg his wife got these books from the heathen army with their pure money, that was with pure gold, for the love of God and for their souls' need, and because they would not have the holy books stay longer in heathen hands, and gave them to Christ Church; our own rendering, not a quotation). Alfred was ealdorman of Surrey; his will survives (S 1508, between 871 and 889). The sum paid is not recorded: thirty mancuses (900 d) is the game's (?). A mancus is thirty pennies. That a boat and a priest went to London for it is invented, and so is the priest Hunsige (Hun- + -sige). Sets ch_great_army_865_6; _gold on 'carry'; _book_home on 'sell'; _book_lost, _cost_church and changed_codex_aureus_lost on 'keep'.

cards.note: Ending 'warned': HISTORY CHANGED (changed_chippenham_warned). At Hamwic from June 878 for the man whose warning was believed. In the Chronicle the king is surprised at Chippenham, hides at Athelney from Easter, wins at Edington in May, and Guthrum is baptised at Aller with the king as godfather. Here the king is ready at Twelfth Night and peace is made at Easter from strength: no Athelney, no Edington, and no baptism (see the chain page for what follows in later years). The king's protection and toll freedom by his writing: the kind of grant English kings made to churches' ships at Lundenwic in the 730s and 740s, here to a layman (?). 1,500 d is six pounds and a quarter. Sets ch_great_army_865_end_warned and ch_great_army_865_done; grand rewards unlock_title_alfreds_protection and unlock_charter_hamwic (and unlock_plot_hamwic on 'land'). The cost that lasts was set at step 10: ch_great_army_865_cost_danes.

cards.note: Ending 'ransomer': WHAT HAPPENED, and the honest road. At Fordwic from June 878 for the man who brought the golden book home. Source: the Codex Aureus inscription (step 6), written above and below the text on the opening of Matthew, with the daughter Alhthryth named beside her parents; the gift to Christ Church, to be read every month for their souls. Freeing a slave at the altar and writing it into a gospel book is English practice, recorded from the 920s (?). Names of friends written into a church's book to be prayed for: the Durham Liber Vitae. Fordwic's toll was the king's, and kings freed minster ships of it (S 29; dossiers/fordwic.md): freedom for a layman's keel at the ealdorman's asking is the game's (?). Forty mancuses is 1,200 d. Sets ch_great_army_865_end_ransomer and ch_great_army_865_done; grand rewards unlock_title_christ_church_friend and unlock_charter_fordwic; on the hard road (the boy ransomed at York and nothing skimmed) twice the silver and unlock_kin_fosterling_wulfric.

cards.note: Ending 'line': WHAT HAPPENED. At Lundenwic from 880 for anyone on the chain. Source: the treaty of Alfred and Guthrum (lore/law_tolls.md 7.2): the border up the Thames and the Lea; clause 5, no slave or free man goes over to the other army without leave, but if they need to trade in cattle and goods it is allowed when hostages are given as a pledge of peace and as proof that a man goes with a clean back (our rendering). The treaty is undated, between 878 and 890, and likely after Alfred took London in 886 (?): the game lets the rule hold from 880, when Guthrum's army settled East Anglia (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 880). A silver bond in place of a living hostage is the game's (economy_and_trade.md) (?). Sets ch_great_army_865_end_line, ch_great_army_865_done and the spine's en_hostage_given; grand reward unlock_title_leave_to_cross (and unlock_factor_gipeswic on 'surety').
